title: Planning
sub: Plugs, the brick table and the choice: sweep or compact
cards/0/body:
The marks are set: the living are separated from the dead. Space can be freed in two ways:

  • Sweep: live objects stay where they are, and the holes between them become free chunks.
  • Compact: live objects slide together, and the free space gathers into one chunk at the end.

Which is better is not known in advance. So between marking and cleanup comes the plan phase: the GC simulates compaction, computing where each live object would move and how much space that would free, and only then decides.
cards/1/body:
The plan walks the condemned generation in order, from lower addresses to higher ones. It can step from object to object because each object's size is known from its MethodTable.

  • Consecutive live objects merge into a plug, which is moved as one piece.
  • Dead objects between plugs form a gap.

For every plug the GC computes a new address: plugs "slide" toward the start, keeping their order. The difference between the old and new address is the relocation distance. It is written right into the gap before the plug: that memory is dead, nobody minds, and no extra memory is needed during the collection.
cards/1/deep: To quickly find the plug for any address later, there is the brick table: the heap is split into "bricks" (4 KB on a 64-bit platform, 2 KB on 32-bit), and for each brick it stores the offset of the root of that brick's plug tree. Plugs within a brick are linked into a binary tree by address. So answering "where did address X move" means: find the brick, walk down the tree, add the relocation distance.
cards/2/q: Why does the GC write plug information into the gap before it rather than into a separate table?
cards/2/options/0: The gap is dead memory that can be overwritten, and nothing new has to be allocated during the collection
cards/2/options/1: It makes the write barrier faster
cards/2/options/2: The GC is not allowed to keep separate tables in the heap
cards/2/options/3: So that an object in the plug knows its new address after the collection
cards/2/explain: A collection often happens exactly when memory is short. Keeping the plan in space that is being freed anyway avoids asking the OS for memory in the middle of a collection.
cards/3/q: Put the phases of a blocking compacting collection in order
cards/3/items/3: Plan: new addresses and the decision
cards/3/explain: First references are rewritten to the new addresses, and only then are objects physically copied. If the plan decides to sweep, sweep runs instead of relocate and compact.
cards/4/title: How the choice is made: sweep or compact
cards/4/body:
Compaction is expensive: copy every survivor and rewrite every reference to it. It pays off only when it frees a lot. The logic is visible in the GC sources: compaction is chosen if:

  • it was demanded: GC.Collect(..., compacting: true), Aggressive mode, a forced-compaction setting;
  • this is the last collection before OutOfMemoryException;
  • fragmentation is high by two measures at once: in bytes and as a share of the generation size;
  • memory load is high, and compacting a full collection would return a noticeable amount;
  • otherwise there would not be enough space for the generations or new allocations.

If none of the conditions holds, it sweeps.
cards/4/deep: This is the decide_on_compacting function in gc.cpp. The fragmentation thresholds live in the generation's dynamic data and depend on the generation and the mode. The GC records the reason in the GCPerHeapHistory trace event (the compaction mechanisms field), and you can inspect it in PerfView.
cards/5/q: When will the plan definitely choose compaction? Select all.
cards/5/options/2: A full collection right before throwing OutOfMemoryException
cards/5/options/3: A plain GC.Collect() with no arguments
cards/5/explain: compacting: true, Aggressive and the collection before OOM turn compaction on explicitly. GC.Collect() with no arguments is a full blocking collection, but the plan itself decides between sweep and compact. For Gen 0 compaction is common but not mandatory.
cards/6/body:
The plan also decides which generation survivors end up in: Gen 0 survivors become Gen 1, Gen 1 survivors become Gen 2.

Then. Before .NET 7 the young generations lived in one contiguous ephemeral segment, and a generation boundary was just an address. Compaction moved objects and boundaries, and that is how survivors "moved" into the older generation.

Now. Since .NET 7 the heap consists of regions, and each region has its own generation. Survivors can be compacted into Gen 1 regions. And if almost everything in a region survived, copying makes no sense: the plan simply moves the whole region to the older generation, sweeping the gaps in place.
cards/6/deep: In the .NET 8 sources such regions are called "swept in plan" (SIP), and the threshold is 90% survival relative to the region size. If almost everything that survived in a region is held by references from Gen 2 (through cards), the region may be moved straight to Gen 2. The threshold is an implementation detail and may change.
cards/7/q: .NET 8. In a Gen 0 region, 95% of objects survived the collection. What will the plan most likely do?
cards/7/options/0: Move the whole region to Gen 1 without copying objects
cards/7/options/1: Copy all the objects into Gen 1 regions
cards/7/options/2: Leave the region in Gen 0 until the next collection
cards/7/explain: Copying 95% of a region to gain 5% of space is a bad deal. The plan labels the region with the new generation and sweeps the holes. Objects do not move, and references to them need no rewriting.
cards/8/body:
A pinned object (fixed, GCHandle with Pinned, the marshaller in P/Invoke) cannot move: native code is looking at its address. The GC records the pinned flag during marking.

The plan is built around such objects: their plug stays in place, and neighboring plugs slide only up to it. The gap before a pinned object does not disappear: it becomes a free chunk, that is, fragmentation.

One short pin costs almost nothing. The trouble is many pinned objects in the young generation: they chop it into pieces. For long pins there is a separate heap since .NET 5, the POH (unit "Advanced").
cards/8/deep: To avoid fragmenting the older generation, the GC may leave a pinned object and its neighbors in the younger generation instead of promoting them; this is called demotion. fixed is cheaper than GCHandle: the JIT just marks the stack slot as pinning in the GC info, and the pin exists only for collections that happen inside the block.
cards/9/q: From which line on can the GC no longer move buf (until Free is called)?
cards/9/explain: The Pinned handle does the pinning. A Span does not pin: it is an interior pointer, and the GC simply rewrites it during compaction. AddrOfPinnedObject only reads the address of an already pinned object.
cards/10/title: LOH and POH: a plan without moving
cards/10/body:
For LOH compaction is not planned by default: copying megabyte-sized arrays is expensive. LOH is swept, and the holes go to the free list.

Exceptions:

  • ask for it once: GCSettings.LargeObjectHeapCompactionMode = GCLargeObjectHeapCompactionMode.CompactOnce; the next blocking full collection compacts LOH, and the mode resets;
  • with a heap hard limit (for example, in a container) and with the GCConserveMemory setting, the GC decides by itself when to compact LOH.

POH is never compacted, and that is its whole point: it holds objects that must not move.
cards/11/q: Compact LOH once, at the next full collection
cards/11/explain: CompactOnce applies to one blocking full collection, after which the mode goes back to Default. GC.Collect() is such a collection right now; without it, compaction happens at the next blocking full one.
